title: Mark
subtitle: the shortest Gospel, in a hurry toward the cross
lead: Mark is the shortest of the four Gospels and, most scholars think, the earliest. It has no birth story and no long sermons. It opens with a voice in the wilderness and a man from Nazareth baptized in the Jordan, and then it runs: "right away" Jesus is tested, calls fishermen, throws out demons, heals, argues, and draws crowds from every side. Halfway through, the story turns toward Jerusalem, and Jesus three times tells his followers that the Son of Man must suffer, die and rise. A third of the book is about his last week. In the oldest manuscripts it ends with women running from an empty tomb, too afraid to speak.

Mark tells the story of God's Son as a story of hiddenness and misunderstanding. Demons know who Jesus is and are silenced; religious leaders call him a blasphemer; his family think he is out of his mind; his own disciples, even Peter, keep failing to understand. The first human to call Jesus God's Son is a Roman soldier watching him die. Written, many think, for a church that knew persecution, Mark asks its readers to follow a crucified Messiah on the way of the cross, and promises that the one who was raised goes ahead of them.
facts: Anonymous. From the early 100s the church named Mark, often identified with John Mark of Jerusalem, a companion of Paul and Barnabas and later of Peter, whose preaching he was said to record. Many critical scholars: an unknown Christian writer; some accept the link with Mark and Peter.
Uncertain. Most scholars: about AD 65–75, around the time of the Jewish war with Rome and the destruction of the Temple (AD 70). Some date it earlier, a few as early as the 40s.
Traditionally Rome, after Nero's persecution of Christians (AD 64). Many scholars suggest Syria or Galilee instead.
A Gospel: a fast-moving account of Jesus' words and deeds, shaped like an ancient biography, with a long passion story at its center.
Greek, plain and vivid, with many Aramaic words translated for the reader and several Latin loanwords.
authorship: Papias, bishop of Hierapolis in Asia Minor early in the 100s, passed on what "the elder" said: that Mark, who had become Peter's interpreter, wrote down accurately, though not in order, all he remembered of what the Lord had said and done; he had not heard the Lord himself but followed Peter, who taught as the needs arose (quoted by Eusebius, Church History 3.39.15). Irenaeus (about 180) says that after the deaths of Peter and Paul, Mark, Peter's disciple and interpreter, handed down in writing what Peter had preached (Against Heresies 3.1.1); Clement of Alexandria places the writing in Rome while Peter was alive (Eusebius, Church History 6.14.6–7). The church identified this Mark with "John, also called Mark," whose mother's house in Jerusalem was a meeting place (Acts 12:12), who traveled with Paul and Barnabas (Acts 12:25; 13:5, 13; 15:37–39), and who was later with Paul (Colossians 4:10; Philemon 24; 2 Timothy 4:11) and with Peter in "Babylon," that is Rome (1 Peter 5:13).

The Gospel itself names no author. Many scholars doubt that it rests on one apostle's memories: it reads as a collection of stories and sayings shaped by years of preaching, some of its geography of Galilee and the Decapolis seems confused (for example 7:31), and Papias' report may have been meant to give the Gospel an apostle's authority. On this view the author was an unknown Christian, perhaps named Mark, a common Roman name. Others (Martin Hengel, Richard Bauckham) defend the tradition: the title was never disputed, and there was no reason to credit a minor figure like Mark unless the link was genuine. Bauckham notes that Peter frames the story (1:16; 16:7) and that the Gospel's viewpoint often follows his.

Chapter 13 is the main clue to the date. Jesus predicts that not one stone of the Temple will be left on another (13:2) and speaks of "the abomination of desolation" standing "where he should not" (13:14, with the aside "let the reader understand"). Scholars who date Mark after AD 70 read these as reflecting the Temple's fall; those who date it before 70 note that the details do not match the Roman siege closely (the Temple burned rather than being torn down stone by stone) and that the warnings fit the years of crisis from Caligula's plan to set up his statue in the Temple (AD 40) to the war of 66–70. Most scholars place Mark close to AD 70; Hengel argued for about 69, Joel Marcus for the years of the war, and James Crossley for the early 40s.

audience.to: A community of believers in Jesus, most of them probably Gentiles, who needed Jewish customs explained (7:3–4) and Aramaic words translated (5:41; 7:34; 15:34), and who knew suffering for their faith. Mark uses Latin loanwords for coins and military terms (kentyriōn for centurion, 15:39; kodrantēs, a Roman coin, 12:42; xestēs, a pot, 7:4; legiōn, 5:9), and once explains a Greek word by a Latin one: the courtyard "that is, the praetorium" (15:16). The traditional view, still the most common, is that these readers were in Rome in the years after Nero blamed Christians for the fire of AD 64 and put many to death.
audience.why: Mark wrote to tell a suffering church the good news of Jesus in a way that explained their own suffering. If the Messiah was rejected, handed over and crucified, then his followers would also be handed over to councils and kings (13:9–13), betrayed by family (13:12) and called to take up the cross (8:34). The failures of the disciples, who misunderstood, fled and denied, offered hope to readers who had failed under pressure: the risen Jesus still goes ahead of them to Galilee (14:28; 16:7), and Peter is named. Knowing this audience explains the urgency of the book, its honesty about weakness, and its focus on the cross. It also explains why Mark explains Jewish ways to outsiders; the debates with Pharisees and scribes are told for Gentile readers who were not part of them.
views: The oldest tradition (Irenaeus; Clement of Alexandria) and many scholars (Martin Hengel; Brian Incigneri) place Mark in Rome. The Latinisms, the explanation of Jewish customs, the theme of persecution and the link with Peter, who died in Rome, all fit. Incigneri argues that Mark answers the trauma of the persecution and the news of the Temple's fall.
Syria or Galilee during the Jewish war

Others (Joel Marcus; Gerd Theissen) place Mark nearer Palestine, perhaps in southern Syria, around the war of AD 66–70. They note Mark's interest in Galilee and its neighbors, the warnings about false messiahs and flight to the mountains (13:14–22), and Latin words that were common in the eastern empire as well. Willi Marxsen proposed Galilee itself.

Richard Bauckham and others argue that the Gospels were written not for one community but to circulate among churches everywhere. On this view the question of Mark's "community" matters less than his intended wide readership of Christians, mostly Gentile, in the Greek-speaking world.

outline: Prologue: John in the wilderness, the baptism, the testing
Authority in Galilee: the first call, a day in Capernaum, five debates
The Twelve, the parables by the lake, mighty works, rejection at Nazareth
The Twelve sent out, John's death, two feedings, bread and blindness
On the way: two blind men frame three predictions of the passion
Jerusalem: the entry, the Temple, the debates, the discourse on the Mount of Olives
The passion: anointing, supper, Gethsemane, trials, crucifixion, burial

lenses.name: History and setting
lenses.desc: Reads Mark against Roman Galilee and Judea, Herod Antipas, the Decapolis and Tyre, and Second Temple Judaism, and asks what can be known of the historical Jesus. Pays attention to Mark's Aramaic words (talitha koum, ephphatha, korban, Abba, Eloi).

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Asks how the Gospel was made: Mark as the source of Matthew and Luke on the majority view, or the minority view that Mark used both; Papias' report of Mark as Peter's interpreter; the date (before or after AD 70), the place (Rome, Syria, Galilee) and the endings.

lenses.name: Literary
lenses.desc: Reads Mark as a story: "right away," the "sandwiches," the messianic secret, disciples who fail to understand, three predictions of the passion, the torn heavens (1:10) and torn curtain (15:38), and the abrupt end at 16:8.

lenses.name: Jewish reading
lenses.desc: Reads Jesus inside first-century Judaism, with Pharisees and scribes as fellow Jews in debate over purity, Sabbath and Temple, using Jewish scholars on Jesus and on Mark (Vermes, Levine, Fredriksen, Boyarin), and notes honestly how passages were later read against Jews.

lenses.name: Church tradition
lenses.desc: How the church fathers, the creeds, the liturgy and the churches have read the passage. Mark was long neglected as a "shortened Matthew" (Augustine), rediscovered in the 1800s as the earliest Gospel, and pictured as the lion among the four living creatures.

sections.b:
Mark is short enough to read aloud in about ninety minutes, and it was probably meant to be heard that way. It moves in three stages. In Galilee (1:14–8:21) Jesus teaches, heals and throws out demons, crowds gather and opposition grows, but no one, not even the disciples, understands who he is. On the way to Jerusalem (8:22–10:52), framed by two healings of blind men, Jesus three times predicts his suffering, death and resurrection (8:31; 9:31; 10:33–34), and each time the disciples misunderstand and are taught what following him means. In Jerusalem (11–16) he enters the city, judges the Temple, debates with its leaders, foretells its fall, and is anointed, betrayed, tried and crucified.

Listen for Mark's habits: "right away" (euthys) more than forty times; the present tense in the middle of past narration; questions that leave the reader thinking ("Who then is this?" 4:41); stories set inside other stories; and a story that ends, in the oldest copies, with the women's fear (16:8).

About ninety percent of Mark's content appears in Matthew, and more than half in Luke, often word for word and in the same order. Most scholars conclude that Mark was written first and that Matthew and Luke used it (Markan priority), together with a collection of sayings (often called Q) or, on the Farrer view, Luke's use of Matthew. A minority holds the Griesbach or Two-Gospel view (William Farmer): Mark combined and shortened Matthew and Luke. For most of church history Mark was thought to be an abridgment of Matthew, following Augustine. The notes point out places where Matthew and Luke differ from Mark in ways that matter for this debate, such as Jesus' anger (1:41; 3:5), the Spirit "throwing" him into the wilderness (1:12), and the omission of Abiathar (2:26). See the topic page on the Synoptic problem.

Jesus in Mark often commands silence: to demons who know him (1:25, 34; 3:12), to people he heals (1:44; 5:43; 7:36; 8:26) and to the disciples after Peter's confession and the transfiguration (8:30; 9:9). He speaks in parables to outsiders (4:11–12). In 1901 William Wrede called this the "messianic secret" and argued that it was a theological device: since Jesus had not been known as Messiah in his lifetime, the tradition explained this by saying he kept it secret. Later scholars have answered in several ways: Jesus really avoided popular titles that would have sounded like a call to revolt; the secret is broken again and again (1:45; 7:36), so it is less about hiding than about the kind of Messiah he is; and Mark ties its end to the cross and resurrection (9:9), since only then can Jesus be rightly understood. See the topic on the Gospel of Mark.

Mark gives the reader the answer in the first line, "Jesus Christ, God's Son" (1:1, with a textual question), and then lets the characters struggle toward it. God calls Jesus his Son at the baptism (1:11) and the transfiguration (9:7). Unclean spirits shout it (3:11; 5:7). Peter names him the Messiah but rejects the suffering that goes with it (8:29–33). Jesus calls himself the Son of Man, who has authority on earth (2:10, 28), who must suffer and give his life as a ransom (8:31; 10:45), and who will come with the clouds (8:38; 13:26; 14:62). At his trial he accepts the titles of Messiah and Son of the Blessed One (14:61–62). The first human to call him God's Son is the centurion at the cross (15:39). Mark also hints at more: Jesus forgives sins, which belongs to God (2:7), stills the sea (4:39–41), walks on it (6:48–50), and is "the Lord" whose road Isaiah promised (1:3).

No Gospel is harder on Jesus' first followers. The Twelve are called, chosen and sent out, but they do not understand the parables (4:13), they fear in the storm (4:40), their hearts are hardened (6:52; 8:17), they argue about greatness after each prediction of the passion (9:33–34; 10:35–41), and in the end one hands him over, all flee, and Peter denies him three times (14:50, 66–72). Yet Mark does not leave them there: the young man at the tomb sends the women to tell "his disciples and Peter" that Jesus goes ahead of them to Galilee (16:7). Readers have seen in this honesty a mark of Peter's own preaching, a warning to the church against pride, and a comfort to believers who had failed under persecution.

The two oldest manuscripts that contain the end of Mark, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus (both 300s), end Mark at 16:8: "they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid." Most later manuscripts add 16:9–20, the "Longer Ending," with appearances of the risen Jesus and the sending of the disciples; a few have a "Shorter Ending" instead or as well. Most scholars think 16:9–20 was added in the 100s, using the other Gospels and Acts, and debate whether Mark meant to end at 16:8, lost his ending, or never finished. This site translates 16:9–20 in full, as nearly all Bibles print it, under a heading that marks it as a later ending; the evidence is set out on the page for chapter 16.

Mark's Greek is plain, repetitive and lively: sentences strung together with "and," double expressions ("as evening came on, when the sun went down," 1:32), and the present tense used for past events. Matthew and Luke often polish it. Mark keeps a number of Aramaic words, Jesus' own language, and translates them: Boanerges (3:17), talitha koum (5:41), korban (7:11), ephphatha (7:34), Abba (14:36), Golgotha (15:22) and the cry Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani (15:34). He also uses Latin loanwords, which have been taken as signs of a Roman setting. The Plain English Translation keeps the Aramaic words where Mark does, with his translations.

Because nearly all of Mark is found in Matthew or Luke, Mark was the least copied, quoted and preached of the four Gospels for most of Christian history. Augustine called Mark Matthew's "follower and abbreviator" (The Harmony of the Gospels 1.2.4). In the 1800s, scholars in Germany and Britain concluded that Mark was the earliest Gospel, and it became the starting point for study of the historical Jesus and, in the late 1900s, for literary readings of the Gospels as stories. In the church's art Mark is the lion among the four living creatures (Ezekiel 1:10; Revelation 4:7), in the assignment Jerome made popular, because the book opens with a voice roaring in the wilderness. The church of Alexandria, and the Coptic Orthodox Church today, honors Mark as its founder (Eusebius, Church History 2.16), and Venice claims his relics, brought from Alexandria in 828.

spec.title: Claude's theory: the reader as the messenger
spec.body: Mark begins with "the beginning of the good news" and with a promise: "Look, I am sending my messenger before your face" (1:2). In the oldest manuscripts he ends with women told to carry a message to the disciples, who say nothing to anyone because they are afraid (16:8). I suggest that the two ends answer each other: the book that opens with a messenger sent ahead of the Lord closes with messengers who fail to speak, leaving the reader holding the message. If so, Mark's open ending is a hand-off. The book is only the "beginning" (1:1), and the reader who has heard the whole story is now the one who must go ahead and tell it. Narrative critics such as David Rhoads, Joanna Dewey and Donald Michie, and many commentators on 16:8, have argued that the ending calls readers to respond where the women did not; linking that call to the messenger of 1:2 is my own suggestion and is speculative.

prompts: The heavens torn open at the Jordan (1:9–11)

A muddy green river between reeds and dry hills; a man in a rough camel-hair garment standing waist-deep, steadying another man who is stepping up out of the water; above them the sky torn open in a jagged rip like torn cloth, with pale light pouring through and a white dove gliding down toward the rising man; a few villagers on the bank shading their eyes, not seeing what he sees.

Style: sketched by hand onto an old rolled parchment scroll. Sepia and iron-gall ink linework with charcoal shading, red-ochre and yellow-ochre pigment like Lascaux cave paintings, a few bold flat shapes of lapis blue in the manner of modern paper cut-outs. Visible parchment grain, uneven hand-drawn lines, soft torn irregular edges that fade into the parchment. No frame, no rectangular border, no sharp corners, no lettering. Wide horizontal composition, 3:2.

A crowded one-room basalt house in a Galilean village, people packed in and spilling out the door; on the flat roof four men have dug a ragged hole through branches and packed clay and are lowering a thin man on a straw mat by ropes; below, a teacher looks up at the man on the mat; scribes in long robes sit along the wall, frowning, while dust falls through the opening in a shaft of light.
